newsitem.title: USA: Elkem silicon metal expansion targets chemicals.
newsitem.headline: Elkem silicon metal expansion targets chemicals.

text.p: Elkem A/S's U.S. metals arm's decision to expand silicon metal output by 20,000 tonnes at its Alloy, West Virginia works will offer little relief to aluminum producers as most of the new metal will be chemical grade for silicones, the company said.
Primary and secondary aluminum or alloy producers consume silicon metal to add certain properties.
Elkem Metal's extra metal will come from a new furnace being started up in the second quarter of 1998, and increased productivity at the company's other four furnaces in West Virginia.
Anthony LaRusso, president of Pittsburgh-based Elkem Metals, said of the 20,000 tonnes, 6,000 tonnes is already coming on stream from improvements at existing furnaces.
La Russo declined to say how much is being invested in the new 14,000 tonne per year furnace, essentially a reconstruction of an existing one.
"This is probably the most economic expansion that we know of anywhere," LaRusso said.
The West Virginia plant will produce 70,000 to 74,000 tonnes of primarily chemical grade silicon metal a year once the new furnace is on stream, La Russo said.

Elkem is already the world's biggest silicon metal producer, and the Norwegian parent said last summer that expansions, including the U.S. project, would raise the company's output to 210,000 tonnes a year, about a quarter of Western world consumption according to the company.
Metallurgical grade silicon metal prices have risen sharply in the past year, peaking in the high 90 cents per pound before easing back to the low 80s at present.

Alloy smelters are annoyed that import dumping duties on metallurgical grade silicon from Brazil and China have made those two countries uncompetitive while U.S. silicon metal producers prefer to make chemical grade because it sells at a higher price.
"We know that the chemical companies are expanding their business and will be needing more silicon in the short-term," one observer said.
LaRusso said dumping duties were a separate issue.
"That's a process that's been gone through with the government and found that the duties are valid," LaRusso added.
Nevertheless, duties leave Russians holding the trump card in the U.S. alloy sector.
"By now 80 to 85 percent of secondary aluminum grade silicon metal is Russian," a Midwest alloy smelter official estimated.
Dumping duties should be lifted to inject more competition into the market, he added, reiterating a longstanding call in the alloy industry.
The Russians were already beginning to wise up to their dominant role in the U.S. alloy sector. "There is some inkling of rising prices from the Russians," the alloy official said.
Metallurgical grade silicon importers were seeking a 1 to 2 cents per pound hike for third quarter shipments, up from 80 to 81 cents in the second quarter, alloy sources said.
